title: Ludiek
excerpt: Ludiek means playful, funny or original. Dutch students use it a lot for silly activities during a KMT or borrel.
example: Going to a lecture dressed up as fruit? They thought that was super ludiek.
text: It comes from the Latin word for game. Students use it for anything funny, playful or creative. Especially during a KMT or borrel, where things are allowed to get a little crazier.

title: Lullepot
excerpt: A lullepot is a made-up story you have to improvise on the spot, often during a KMT.
example: At the last second she had to invent a lullepot about a word she had just drawn.
text: The story is usually about a set topic, or has to include a few fixed words. New members often get asked to do one during the KMT. The result can be hilarious. Or a total disaster, which is also hilarious.

title: Lurking
excerpt: Lurking means reading and watching online without posting or reacting yourself.
example: "I've been in that group chat for years, but I've never sent anything. I'm just lurking."
text: A lurker sees a lot of content, but stays almost invisible. In group chats, forums or on social media. There is nothing wrong with it. Lots of people prefer lurking over posting themselves.

title: Lustrum
excerpt: A lustrum is a five-year anniversary of a Dutch association, usually celebrated with a trip or a gala.
example: For the lustrum of the association they organised a whole trip to Barcelona.
text: Every five years a Dutch student association celebrates big. Think of a lustrum trip, a lustrum gala and often a whole week of events. Some even celebrate a midlustrum after two and a half years. Any excuse for a party.

title: M
excerpt: M is Dutch slang for the drug MDMA, the active ingredient in ecstasy.
example: At the festival people were whispering about whether anyone still had M.
text: The letter is mostly used around parties and festivals as a short way to say MDMA. In English you might hear molly. Pills of the same stuff are called X. If you ever use, know that drug testing services exist in the Netherlands. Safety first.

title: Maat
excerpt: Maat is a Dutch word for mate or buddy.
example: "Thanks maat, that really helped," he said to his housemate, relieved.
text: Students use it in almost every casual situation to talk to a friend. It works just like "mate" in British English. Close relatives: kompaan and gozer.

title: Main character
excerpt: Being the main character means acting like the world revolves around you. Sometimes a compliment, sometimes not.
example: "She cycled through the rain with her headphones on like she was in a film. Main character energy."
text: The term got big on TikTok around 2020. In a positive way it is about enjoying your own life. In a negative way it is about someone self-centred who wants all the attention. The opposite is an NPC.

title: Major
excerpt: A major is your main field of study, especially in the American system.
example: "My major is economics, but I also take philosophy courses."
text: In the US you pick a major and often a minor too. The major is the biggest part of your degree. Dutch university colleges work the same way. At other Dutch universities you just call it your programme.

title: Matras
excerpt: Matras (mattress) is a not very nice Dutch student word for someone who sleeps with a lot of different people.
example: Behind his back people sometimes giggled and called him a matras.
text: It is mostly used in gossip within a friend group or house. Definitely not a compliment. Calling someone that to their face is out of pocket.

title: Mattie
excerpt: Mattie is Dutch youth slang for a friend. Used by young people everywhere, not just students.
example: "Yo mattie, are you coming tonight?" he texted his best friend.
text: It is used widely among young people in the Netherlands, not just at universities. Just as normal as maat or kompaan. A bit more street, a bit more Amsterdam.

title: MC
excerpt: MC (Marie-Claire) is the stereotypical female corps student: flared jeans, a hair clip and a bottle of wine.
example: With her flared jeans and hair clip she looked like a real MC.
text: The cliché is flared jeans, a claw clip, a membership of the corps and always a bottle of wine at hand. Of course not every Marie-Claire fits the picture. The male version is the bal.

title: MDM
excerpt: MDM stands for "met de meiden" or "met de mannen": a night with your small, trusted group of girls or guys.
example: "Cosy MDM tonight," she texted her best friends before opening a bottle of wine.
text: You use it when you do something with your close group. A glass of wine with the girls, watching football with the guys. Small group, no strangers, maximum gezelligheid.

title: Medium
excerpt: Among Dutch students, medium means "okay, but not great".
example: "How was the party?" "Meh, medium," he answered with a shrug.
text: You say it when something wasn't bad, but definitely wasn't great either. Right in the middle. The English slang word mid means pretty much the same.

title: Meme
excerpt: A meme is an image, video or phrase that spreads online and keeps getting changed and shared.
example: "Someone turned a photo of our praeses into a meme. Now it's in every group chat."
text: Memes work because everyone recognises the format. You adapt it to a new situation and share it again. They are a huge part of internet culture. Some memes stay popular for years, others for a week.

title: Meter bier
excerpt: A meter bier (metre of beer) is a wooden plank with exactly eleven small beers on it, served in some Dutch bars.
example: For the birthday they ordered a whole meter bier for the table right away.
text: It is a fun way to order a round for a group. Disputen often have their own meter as part of their gear, though theirs doesn't always hold eleven beers. Finishing one alone is a challenge. Finishing one together is gezellig.

title: Micro-cheating
excerpt: Micro-cheating is small stuff that crosses lines in a relationship, without being actual cheating.
example: "He has a girlfriend, but texts his ex flirty messages every night. Isn't that micro-cheating?"
text: Think of secret texting, liking photos with hearts or keeping your relationship quiet. There is no fixed list. What counts is what you agreed on together. Talking about it saves a lot of fights.

title: Mid
excerpt: Mid means average. Not bad, but definitely not good either. Just meh.
example: "Everyone was so excited about that new film, but honestly? It was mid."
text: Mid is often harsher than bad. Something bad at least makes you feel something. Something mid is just forgettable. You hear it about food, music, parties and sometimes people's looks. The Dutch say medium.

title: Miemelen
excerpt: Miemelen is Dutch slang for whining or moaning.
example: "Stop miemelen and grab another beer," she said, laughing.
text: You mostly use it when someone is complaining about something small that doesn't need to be taken too seriously. Every student house has someone who loves to miemelen about the dishes.

title: Minor
excerpt: A minor is a secondary subject or block of courses you take next to your main programme.
example: "I'm doing my minor in Barcelona. Officially to study, of course."
text: A minor has fewer courses than a major. You dive into another topic or go deeper into your own field. In the Netherlands many students do their minor in their third year, sometimes abroad.

title: Mood
excerpt: You say mood when something fits exactly how you feel. Totally relatable.
example: She sent a photo of a cat hiding under a blanket. Her friend replied: "Mood."
text: With mood you show you completely recognise yourself in a photo, meme or situation. You can also say it about the vibe of a place or music. A big mood is something extremely relatable.

title: Mores
excerpt: Mores are the unwritten rules within a Dutch student association or dispuut.
example: "That really goes against the mores of our association," the praeses said sternly.
text: Breaking the mores doesn't come with official punishments, like breaking the house rules does. But people will definitely let you know. The word is Latin. The singular, for the nerds, is mos.

title: Nakkie
excerpt: A nakkie is Dutch slang for a line of drugs.
example: At the party someone was secretly taking a nakkie in the toilet.
text: The word mostly comes up in stories about festivals or parties where drugs go around. In English you would say a line. Not something to be proud of, and definitely not something to mix with a lot of alcohol.

title: Nekken
excerpt: Nekken means downing a drink in one go.
example: "You lost, so now you have to nekken that shot," she grinned.
text: It literally means "necking", and works just like the British slang. Dutch students use it interchangeably with adten or bak trekken. Same thing every time: the drink goes down in one gulp.

title: NGL
excerpt: NGL stands for not gonna lie. Honestly.
example: "NGL, I expected this party to be way more boring."
text: You put NGL in front of an honest opinion or confession. It makes what you say feel light and casual. It is close to TBH.

title: Night out
excerpt: A night out is an evening away from home, just for fun.
example: "After this exam week we really need a night out."
text: A night out can be anything. Dinner, a concert, bars or clubbing. It often starts with pre-drinks and ends at the snack bar. The next morning sometimes comes with a serious hangover.

title: Nominaal lopen
excerpt: Nominaal lopen means passing all the credits of your study year on time.
example: Despite all the borrels he still managed to stay nominaal this year.
text: It means getting every credit of a block or study year on time, without delays or resits. Dutch parents love to hear it. Dutch students who also do a board year or a lot of committees rarely manage it.

title: Normi
excerpt: Normi is Dutch slang for normal. Short for "normaal".
example: "Just act normi," she said when he was being over the top again.
text: It is used to say someone or something is just normal, without exaggerating. The Dutch love the phrase "doe normaal", which means calm down and act normal. Normi is the student version.

title: NPC
excerpt: An NPC is someone who doesn't seem to have their own opinion and just goes along with everyone else.
example: "He just repeats whatever his feed tells him. Real NPC behaviour."
text: NPC stands for non-player character. In games those are the characters no player controls, who keep saying the same things. Calling someone an NPC means they are predictable and boring. The opposite is the main character.

title: Nul
excerpt: A nul (zero) is a first-year student who isn't a full member of a Dutch student association yet.
example: As a nul she had to accept every drink from the older members that night.
text: Some associations use nul instead of feut for someone who isn't a full member yet. You start at zero. Literally. After the introduction period you count.

title: Office hours
excerpt: Office hours are set times when students can drop by a teacher with questions.
example: "I don't get this formula at all. I'm going to the professor's office hours tomorrow."
text: During office hours you can ask questions about the material, get feedback or discuss your research. You don't need a separate appointment. Lots of students use them way too little.

title: OMW
excerpt: OMW stands for on my way.
example: "OMW!" he texted at nine. At half past nine he was still in the shower.
text: You send OMW when you leave or are almost there. Sometimes it is a bit optimistic and you haven't even left the house. Everyone knows that. Everyone still sends it.

title: One-night stand
excerpt: A one-night stand is sex for one night only, with no strings attached.
example: They had agreed beforehand that it would stay a one-night stand.
text: Most one-night stands happen after a night out, but it can also happen with a friend. Afterwards there is often a walk of shame home in last night's clothes.

title: Ontgroening
excerpt: Ontgroening is the old name for the introduction period of a Dutch student association. These days it is officially called KMT.
example: Back in the day everyone called it ontgroening. Now it's officially the KMT.
text: It literally means "de-greening": getting rid of your newness. Besides the ontgroening of an association, some student houses have their own house version. You have to get through it to officially get your room. The rules are much stricter these days than they used to be.

title: OOTD
excerpt: OOTD stands for Outfit Of The Day. You show what you are wearing today.
example: She posted a mirror selfie before the gala with the caption: "OOTD."
text: You see OOTD in captions and videos about fashion and lifestyle. You share your outfit, from everyday to fancy. It is close to a fit check. Someone who always looks good has drip.

title: Orbiting
excerpt: Orbiting is when someone stops talking to you, but keeps following and watching your social media.
example: "He ghosted me, but he still watches every single story. He's orbiting."
text: The person circles around you like a planet, without ever really reaching out. Likes, views and maybe a reaction. But never an actual conversation. It often comes after ghosting.

title: Out of pocket
excerpt: Out of pocket means inappropriate, over the line or unexpectedly shocking.
example: "At the first dinner with her parents he asked about her body count. Totally out of pocket."
text: You say it when someone crosses a social line. A comment, joke or question that makes no sense. In other situations out of pocket means something you pay yourself. That is a completely different meaning.

title: P
excerpt: P is Dutch student slang for the propedeuse, the certificate you get after passing your first year.
example: "Did you get your P yet?" her mum asked at the end of the year.
text: It is pronounced "pay" and is a lot shorter than saying propedeuse every time. Getting your P is a big moment. It means you survived year one, and the BSA can't touch you anymore.

title: Pabo
excerpt: Pabo is the Dutch teacher training college for primary school. Among students it also means a parkborrel: drinks in the park.
example: When the weather was nice they spontaneously threw a pabo in the park near the sociëteit.
text: As a degree, pabo stands for the teacher training programme for primary education. In student slang the same word means parkborrel. A crate, some friends and the first sun of the year. Both are very Dutch.

title: Paklijst
excerpt: The paklijst (packing list) is the list of often random items you have to bring at the start of the KMT.
example: The paklijst included a rubber chicken and an empty jam jar, among other things.
text: The paklijst is a fixed tradition at the start of every KMT. The items range from practical to completely absurd. Nobody tells you why you need a rubber chicken. You will find out.

title: Pandapunten
excerpt: Pandapunten (panda points) count how many weeks a student hasn't had sex.
example: "I'm on eight pandapunten by now," he said with mixed pride.
text: For every week without sex you earn a panda point. Collect a lot and your house will crown you the huispanda. The opposite scoring system is called tijgerpunten.

title: Para
excerpt: Para is Dutch slang for paracetamol, for the headache after a night of drinking.
example: Before going to sleep she quickly took a para for the headache she knew was coming.
text: It helps against headaches. But more doesn't mean better, and it is not a cure for drinking too much. Water and sleep do most of the work. The other student favourite is ibu.

title: Parasocial relationship
excerpt: A parasocial relationship is a one-sided bond with a famous person or creator you don't actually know.
example: "She calls that streamer her best friend. She's never met him." That's a parasocial relationship.
text: Social media makes these bonds feel extra personal. Creators share their daily lives and talk straight into the camera. So it feels like you know them. But they have no idea who you are.

title: Party animal
excerpt: A party animal is someone who loves going out, partying and always wants to be there.
example: "Out four nights a week and still in class at nine. A real party animal."
text: A party animal has lots of energy and loves nightlife. It isn't about how much someone drinks, but about how much they love a party. Every association has a few. Dutch students call going hard tetteren.

title: Pauper
excerpt: Pauper is a Dutch word for someone without manners, used by people who think they are a bit better.
example: "Don't be such a pauper at the table," she hissed at her little brother.
text: In English a pauper is a very poor person. In Dutch student slang it is more about manners than money. It is often said with a bit of mockery. A close cousin is proleet.

title: Pechgeneratie
excerpt: The pechgeneratie (unlucky generation) are the Dutch students who studied under the loan system, without the old free grant.
example: As a typical member of the pechgeneratie, he had to borrow everything from DUO.
text: From 2015 the free grant of about 280 euros a month for students living away from home disappeared. So this group had to borrow everything. The grant came back in 2023, which made the pechgeneratie feel even unluckier.

title: Period
excerpt: You put period after a statement to say: full stop, nothing more to discuss.
example: "She's the best housemate we've ever had. Period."
text: Period is the American word for a full stop. Online people also write "periodt" for extra emphasis. You use it to show you are sure of your opinion. It is close to facts.

title: Photo dump
excerpt: A photo dump is a post with a loose collection of photos from a trip, month or night.
example: "I posted a photo dump from the ski trip. Twenty photos, half of them food."
text: A photo dump is less polished than one perfect picture on purpose. Nice photos sit next to random moments. That is what makes it personal. It is a popular way to post on Instagram.

title: Pick-me
excerpt: A pick-me is someone who does everything to get approval, especially from the opposite sex.
example: "I'm not like other girls, I just drink beer with the guys." Classic pick-me.
text: A pick-me likes to set themselves apart from everyone else, sometimes by putting others down. The term is mostly used for pick-me girls, but pick-me boys exist too. The behaviour is usually seen as cringe.

title: Pint
excerpt: Among Flemish students, a pint is simply a beer.
example: On a terrace in Ghent he ordered a pint without hesitating.
text: In Belgium a pint usually means a regular glass of lager, not the big British pint. Dutch students just say biertje. Same drink, different word, depending on which side of the border you are.

title: Pinten harken
excerpt: Pinten harken (raking pints) means drinking a lot of beers in a row.
example: He spent the whole night at the bar pinten harken with his jaarclub.
text: Also called pilsjes harken. It is a lot like bakken vouwen: lots of beer in a short time. Something heavyweights are proud of. Their Sunday usually isn't.
